topic: Comparing models and making qualified data-based inferences
subtitle: Comparing models and qualifying what the data supports

problems.desc: Part (b) rubric: the survey covered only grades 9 and 10 at one school, so the proportion 13/40 describes those 200 students and, if they were a random sample of the two grades, can be extended with caution to all grade 9 and 10 students at that school. It cannot be extended to the whole school (grades 11 and 12 were never asked) or to students elsewhere. Full credit names the population the figure does describe AND at least one group it does not. Do not accept a bare 'the sample is too small' -- 200 is not the problem here; coverage is.

Part (b) rubric: the mean is 10 mm and the median is 8 mm, and the gap exists because the single 27 mm day pulls the mean up while the median barely moves. A typical day is better described by the median, and the matching spread to quote with it is the interquartile range rather than the standard deviation. Full credit names the 27 mm value as the reason the two summaries disagree and chooses the median with a reason. Accept a defence of the mean only if it acknowledges the outlier and says why the total still matters.
problems.slot: (b) which summary describes a typical day

problems.desc: Rubric: a correlation between weekly hours of screen time and reading score, however strong, cannot establish that screen time causes lower scores, because the data are observational -- nobody assigned the hours. A third variable could drive both; acceptable confounders include hours of sleep, family income, or how much time is available for reading in the first place. Reverse causation is also open: weaker readers may choose screens over books. Full credit states that observational data cannot establish causation AND names one plausible confounding variable. Do not accept 'correlation is not causation' with no variable named and no reason.

problems.slot: (a) the sum of squared residuals for Model B

problems.desc: Part (b) rubric: Model A has the smaller sum of squared residuals, 1.39 against 5.5, so it fits the six observed weeks better. The qualification that must appear is that a better fit over weeks 1 to 6 is not by itself a reason to trust either line at week 20 -- that is extrapolation far outside the data, and a plant's growth is not linear forever. Full credit picks Model A with the two numbers as evidence AND states the extrapolation caveat. Award partial credit for the choice alone.
problems.slot: (b) which model fits better, and what that does not license

problems.desc: Part (c) rubric: the two conditional proportions are 2/5 for grade 9 and 1/4 for grade 10, so within this survey a larger share of grade 9 students took the bus. The response must stop there: with 100 students in each grade and no measure of how much such a gap varies from survey to survey, a difference of this size is a description of these respondents, not evidence that grade 9 students in general prefer the bus. Full credit reports the comparison in the right direction AND declines to generalise, with a reason. Do not accept a flat 'grade 9 students prefer the bus'.

problems.slot: (a) the gap between the two predictions

problems.desc: Part (b) rubric: a defensible conclusion says that over weeks 1 to 6 the plant's height rose at roughly 3 cm per week and that a straight line describes the six measurements closely, with Model A the closer of the two. The required qualification is any one of: the models were fitted to six points from a single plant, so they say nothing about plants in general; week 8 is outside the observed range and the two models already disagree there by about 0.9 cm, a gap that widens further out; or growth cannot stay linear indefinitely. Full credit is a claim the data supports plus one genuine qualification, in two sentences. An unqualified prediction for week 20 earns nothing.
